title: Round 2: Diagnose a slow API with database and infrastructure symptoms
description: Learn a repeatable framework for diagnosing slow APIs when the symptoms point to database queries, resource contention, or infrastructure bottlenecks.

data.text: A user reports that a page loads slowly. The API endpoint in question returns data from a database, and the problem gets worse as traffic grows. Your job is to walk the interviewer through how you would investigate and fix the issue without guessing.

items: Reproduce the symptom: confirm the latency with monitoring tools and identify the exact endpoint.
Measure the layers: database query time, network transfer time, API processing time, and client-side rendering time.
Check resource utilization: CPU, memory, disk I/O, and network on both the database server and the API server.
Isolate the cause: determine whether the bottleneck is the query, the connection pool, the code, or the infrastructure.
Fix and verify: implement a change, measure the impact, and decide whether the fix is complete or if it introduced a new bottleneck.

data.text: The most common database culprit is a query that scans too many rows. An index can reduce that scan, but adding an index also affects writes and storage. You need to justify the index choice with actual query plans and frequency of use.

data.title: Query plan hint
data.content: In SQL Server, an index seek on the filter column usually beats an index scan for selective queries:

rows: Connection pool exhaustion or lock contention
Check pool usage and wait stats
One query is slow, others are fast
CPU is high on the DB server
Identify the top queries by CPU
Check disk queue length and memory grants

data.title: Start with measurements
data.text: Never fix a performance issue based on instinct. Use APM tools, database query plans, and infrastructure metrics to build a timeline that shows when the slowdown started and what changed around that time.

data.title: Summary
points: Use a layered measurement approach: client, network, API, and database
Prefer targeted database changes over broad infrastructure upgrades
Verify the fix with the same monitoring data that revealed the problem
data.takeaway: A disciplined diagnostic process is more valuable than a quick guess. Interviewers want to see your reasoning, not just your answer.
